title: Ramana's Forty Verses
hook: movie night: the sheet ripples and everyone sees the screen
tomorrow: how much would you have to know to be called wise?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana's Forty Verses set aside the real-or-illusion fight to ask who's looking. Today, a movie.

Senior movie night on the football field. A white sheet strung between the goalposts, a projector on a folding table, blankets everywhere. The film is halfway through, a car chase, then a rescue, and nobody has looked at the sheet once. Then the wind picks up. The sheet ripples. For a second the hero's face bends like water, and the whole field laughs, because suddenly everyone can see the thing the movie was on the whole time.
screen: `MOVIE NIGHT ON THE FIELD.` → `NOBODY LOOKS AT THE SHEET.` → `THE WIND, AND THE SCREEN SHOWS.`

segments.voice: Ramana's first verse uses exactly this picture. In paraphrase: since we see a world, we accept one source with many powers. The picture of names and forms, nama-rupa, the one who watches it, the screen, and the light that makes it visible: all of these are that one. A few verses on, he looks closer. The world, he says, is five kinds of sensing: sight, sound, smell, taste and touch, known by the mind, manas, through the senses. So, apart from the mind, is there a world? It's easy to stop there and hear: it's all in your head. He doesn't stop there. The world and the mind, the next verse says, rise together and set together. In deep sleep both go quiet; on waking both come back. But that in which both rise and set, the fullness that doesn't come and go: that is what is. Here's the twist worth repeating. The mind isn't the screen. It's part of the movie. The verses point behind the viewer too, to what was there before the lights went down, and is still there after the credits.
screen: `NAMES AND FORMS, AND A SCREEN.` · `THE WORLD: FIVE KINDS OF SENSING.` · `WORLD AND MIND RISE TOGETHER.` · `THE MIND IS PART OF THE MOVIE.` · then, large: `WHAT BOTH APPEAR IN, IS.`

segments.voice: Let sounds come to you for the sit: a fan, traffic, your own breath. Each one starts and fades. Instead of following them, rest in the quiet they show up in, the way the sheet holds every scene.
Ramana's Forty Verses: a Tamil poem that begins with a picture show and asks about the screen.
The line to take with you: Ramana's Forty Verses. Every movie plays on something nobody watches.

howItsDone: Readers of Ramana often use the screen-and-picture image when they talk about his teaching, and his followers sit with the first verse as an entry into the poem.
